question:
Patient note:
A 29-year-old woman employed as a pastry chef was referred to the pre-operative medicine service this afternoon by general surgery for clearance before a scheduled laparoscopic cholecystectomy to treat symptomatic biliary colic; she walked from the bus stop carrying a small backpack and spoke in full sentences without distress. She explains that gallbladder discomfort began eight months ago and has intensified despite low-fat dietary adjustments, yet she remains able to complete ten-hour shifts that involve standing at a commercial mixer, rolling dough, and lifting 25-lb bags of flour. Her medical history is notable for a childhood diagnosis of allergic asthma that evolved into persistent bronchial hyper-reactivity during adolescence. Over the past three years she has required twice-daily inhalations of a budesonide–formoterol combination (160/4.5 µg) and a morning tiotropium capsule to keep symptoms in check; she keeps an albuterol metered-dose inhaler in her apron and typically uses two puffs once or twice per week when the kitchen becomes smoky, but she has not visited an emergency department or needed oral prednisone for more than two years. Office spirometry obtained by pulmonary medicine last month demonstrated an FEV1 of 2.3 L (68 % predicted) with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.60 and less than 10 % reversibility after bronchodilator, and a posteroanterior chest radiograph on the same day showed clear parenchyma and flattened diaphragms without infiltrate. Six years ago during a community testing event she learned she was living with human immunodeficiency virus; the infection was discovered late, and an initial laboratory panel at that time documented a CD4 count of 94 cells/µL and HIV-1 RNA above 500,000 copies/mL. Shortly thereafter she developed a three-week course of Pneumocystis pneumonia that responded to trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, and antiretroviral therapy with bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide was begun during the same hospitalization. Adherence has been excellent—pharmacy refills are on time, resistance testing showed no mutations, and her most recent viral load last month was undetectable with a CD4 recovery to 322 cells/µL—yet she remains vigilant about prophylaxis and keeps annual pneumococcal and influenza vaccinations up to date. She has never been diagnosed with hepatitis B or C, denies jaundice, pruritus, abdominal swelling, easy bruising, or previous abnormal coagulation studies, and a comprehensive metabolic panel drawn two weeks ago revealed alanine aminotransferase 19 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 22 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 74 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 4.3 g/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.0. She reports no episodes of substernal pressure, palpitations, exertional diaphoresis beyond normal exertion, orthopnea, nocturnal dyspnea, or ankle swelling; she jogged two miles on a riverside trail last weekend at a conversational pace without chest tightness or leg cramps. A screening electrocardiogram performed during an employee physical last year showed normal sinus rhythm, axis within normal limits, and no Q waves or ST-segment deviations. She has never been hospitalized for heart failure, never required diuretics, and has no family history of premature coronary artery disease. Neurologically she denies episodes of facial droop, unilateral weakness, transient speech disturbance, visual obscurations, seizures, or balance problems; she manages complex bakery finances on a spreadsheet and recalls ingredient weights from memory. Vascular review is likewise uneventful: she has no calf pain when hurrying to catch the bus, no color change in her toes, and pedal pulses have always been palpable. Endocrine history is free of hyperglycemia; fasting glucose measured at last week’s clinic visit was 93 mg/dL, and hemoglobin A1c has remained between 5.1 % and 5.4 % on annual screens, so she has never required dietary counseling for carbohydrate restriction or pharmacologic glucose control. Renal function today is normal with sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 12 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, yielding an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 110 mL/min/1.73 m²; urinalysis is bland with no protein, blood, or casts. She denies peptic discomfort, chronic reflux, hematemesis, melena, or prior endoscopic therapy and uses only pantoprazole 20 mg as needed for occasional heartburn after tasting high-fat batter. Past surgical history is limited to insertion of a levonorgestrel intrauterine device five years ago under local anesthesia without complication. Medications include the inhalers noted, antiretroviral fixed-dose combination one tablet nightly, cholecalciferol 2000 IU daily, and acetaminophen 650 mg sparingly for biliary pain; she takes no non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and reports no drug allergies. She quit smoking at 21 after accumulating seven pack-years, does not vape, drinks a glass of red wine on birthdays only, and denies recreational drug use. Both parents are alive and healthy in their mid-fifties; there is no family history of stroke, deep-vein thrombosis, inflammatory bowel disease, or malignancy before age 60. Review of systems today is negative for fever, night sweats, weight loss, cough, hemoptysis, wheeze beyond baseline, dyspnea at rest, dysuria, gross hematuria, rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, or arthralgia. On examination she appears lean, alert, and in no acute distress. Vital signs: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 114/70 mm Hg seated in the left arm, heart rate 76 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 15 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 97 % breathing ambient air, and body-mass index 22 kg/m². Skin is warm without cyanosis or clubbing; oropharynx is clear with no thrush. Neck is supple, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, jugular venous pulsation is 3 cm above the sternal angle at 45 °, and the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced. S1 and S2 are crisp with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs demonstrate mild expiratory wheezes diffusely but good air entry and no crackles. Abdomen is flat and mildly tender in the right upper quadrant without rebound or guarding; Murphy sign is equivocal, liver edge is smooth and non-tender, spleen is not palpable, and there is no ascites. Extremities are warm with 2+ radial, femoral, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally, capillary refill under two seconds, and no edema or varicosities. Neurologic exam shows intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength throughout, symmetric reflexes, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and steady tandem gait. Surgical colleagues request confirmation that her respiratory status and immunologic condition will permit an outpatient laparoscopic procedure, guidance on peri-operative antimicrobial prophylaxis in the context of past opportunistic infection, and advice regarding safe intervals to resume heavy lifting in the bakery after cholecystectomy.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums weighted chronic diagnoses. The age-adjusted version adds no age points below 50, so either version gives the same result here.
- Chronic pulmonary disease (1 point): persistent asthma requiring daily maintenance inhalers, with FEV1 68% predicted and FEV1/FVC 0.60 → 1.
- AIDS (6 points): prior Pneumocystis pneumonia was an AIDS-defining illness, and her CD4 nadir was 94/µL. Current viral suppression and CD4 recovery do not erase that history → 6.
- Other CCI diagnoses: no documented myocardial infarction, heart failure, peripheral or cerebrovascular disease, dementia, connective tissue disease, peptic ulcer, chronic liver disease, diabetes, hemiplegia, qualifying renal disease, or malignancy → 0 each. Biliary colic is not a CCI diagnosis.
- Age 29 → 0.
Sum: 1 + 6 + 0 + 0 = 7.
Final answer: 7
